AI in RStudio October 11, 2026 About this Book This book is a beginner’s guide to getting started with AI in RStudio on AnVIL. This book is part of a series of books for the Genomic Data Science Analysis, Visualization, and Informatics Lab-space (AnVIL) of the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI). Learn more about AnVIL by visiting https://anvilproject.org or reading the article in Cell Genomics. Skills Level Cloud & AI knowledge Beginner: prior cloud computing or local AI experiences are helpful but not required Data Analysis Beginner: no prior RNA-seq data analysis experience is needed Programming skills Novice: no programming experience needed AnVIL Collection Please check out our full collection of AnVIL and related resources: https://hutchdatascience.org/AnVIL_Collection/

Learning Objectives Provision GPU-accelerated cloud infrastructure and deploy local AI models with Ollama in RStudio on AnVIL. Use ellmer to connect R to LLMs and leverage gander for context-aware data exploration and coding in RStudio on AnVIL. Use gander to drive RNA-seq data exploration and analysis with tidyverse and DESeq2 on AnVIL.

Chapter 2 Run Local Models Running Local AI Models with RStudio and Ollama 2.1 Learning Objectives Provision infrastructure: Configure and launch a GPU-accelerated RStudio environment on AnVIL. Deploy local AI: Install and run an Ollama server locally, and download qwen3-coder model. Integrate with R: Connect R to the local AI server via ellmer. 2.2 RStudio Setup with GPU on AnVIL Before you can interact with local AI models, you must provision a cloud-based RStudio environment on AnVIL equipped with adequate hardware. 2.2.1 Open the workspace and configure compute settings In AnVIL, navigate to your workspace. Click on the cloud icon on the far right to view Cloud Environment options. In the dialog box, under RStudio, click Settings. Configure: Parameter Selection Application RStudio CPUs 8 Memory 52 GB GPU configuration Enable GPUs (toggle ON) GPU type NVIDIA Tesla T4 Number of GPUs 1 Read and review the estimated hourly running cost displayed in the dialog. Scroll down and click CREATE. The GPU type and the configuration options above are what AnVIL offered when this document was written. Available GPU types and configurations may change as GPU options on AnVIL evolve. The basic recommendation is to enable the smallest GPU option that comfortably holds your LLM model. 2.2.2 Launch RStudio When your environment is ready, its status will change to green (Running). Click the RStudio icon, then Open. RStudio will open in a new browser tab. 2.3 Setup Local AI model With your RStudio environment successfully providioned, the next step is to setup the local AI server and download the model. Here, we will use the Ollama server and pull the qwen3-coder:30b model. 2.3.1 Install Ollama server and download the model In RStudio, click the Terminal tab next to the Console tab. All commands in this section must be executed in the Terminal (not inside R Console). Install the server and pull the model by running this code in the Terminal. # 1. Download the local Ollama server into a folder mkdir ollama curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/download/ollama-linux-amd64.tar.zst | tar x --zstd -C ollama # 2. Launch the server in the background, logging to a file nohup ollama/bin/ollama serve > ollama.log 2>&1 & # 3. Pull (download) the model ollama/bin/ollama pull qwen3-coder:30b Ollama may unload the model from memory after 5 or more minutes of inactivity.  To keep the model in memory you can set the environment variable OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE=-1. If you don’t keep Ollama ‘alive’, after inactivity, you may need to pull the model again in the Terminal like so: ollama/bin/ollama pull qwen3-coder:30b. Do a test prompt and wait for the response. ollama/bin/ollama run qwen3-coder:30b "Say hi" NOTE - The first response may take more than a minute (subsequent responses will be faster). You can check by running the same test prompt a second time and noting the increase in the speed of the response. TIP - If the first prompt response is taking too long, CANCEL the command (Command + C on Mac), and then re-run the command. This will typically fix the response hold-up. Check if GPU is active: ollama/bin/ollama ps Example terminal output: NAME ID SIZE PROCESSOR CONTEXT UNTIL qwen3-coder:30b 06c1097efce0 19 GB 25%/75% CPU/GPU 4096 About a minute from now 2.3.2 Connect R to the local AI server All commands in this section must be executed in the R Console (not inside Terminal). Install and load required packages by running the following code in the R Console: # AI integration packages install.packages( "ellmer") library(ellmer) Connect R to your local AI server by running the following code in the R Console: ellmer provides the R functions that let you connect to and communicate with your local AI server from R. Make sure you have installed and loaded ellmer before continuing. chat <- chat_ollama( base_url = Sys.getenv("ollama/bin/ollama", "http://localhost:11434"), model = "qwen3-coder:30b", ) Notice how you didn’t need to specifically evoke ellmer via ellmer::chat_ollama()? This is because you had already loaded the package into your session using library(ellmer), which makes its functions directly available in your current environment. Alternatively, you could code explicitly: `chat <- ellmer::chat_ollama(...). Test the connection by asking AI a question chat$chat("Tell me one short fact about human genome") 2.3.3 Quiz Ask AI a question using chat$chat and paste question and answer below? Question: Answer: Why does enabling a GPU matter for this workshop? A. DESeq2 requires a GPU. B. The large language model (LLM) is hosted locally and runs much faster on a GPU. C. It speeds up the cloud storage data transfer during the bucket copy process. D. It is required by AnVIL on RStudio. Correct Answer: B (The LLM is hosted locally and generates responses much faster on a GPU.) You provision an RStudio instance with 8 CPUs, 52 GB of system memory, and 1 NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU (16 GB VRAM). You plan to load a 19 GB model (e.g. qwen3-coder). What will happen when you load the model? A. The model will fit entirely within the 16 GB VRAM of the Tesla T4 GPU. B. The model will fail to load completely because it exceeds the total system memory of 52 GB. C. The application will automatically split the model layers between the GPU and the CPU system memory, allowing it to run successfully despite being slower than a fully resident model. D. The environment will automatically upgrade your hardware to a larger GPU to accommodate the full 19 GB model in VRAM. Correct Answer: C (Because the ~19 GB model exceeds the Tesla T4’s 16 GB VRAM capacity, the model cannot fit entirely on the graphics card and automatically offloads the remaining layers to the CPU, allowing the model to run successfully even though it will be slower than a fully GPU-resident model.) What is the primary purpose of running the “nohup” command? A. To run the Ollama server in the background, keeping it alive even if the terminal session ends or the tab is closed, while redirecting output to a log file. B. To automatically update the server to the latest version and pin the release for workshop reproducibility. C. To force the 19 GB model download to run concurrently with the server startup. D. To execute the server commands directly inside the R Console without throwing an error. Correct Answer: A (nohup (no hangup) combined with the trailing & allows the process to continue running in the background after the terminal session closes, preventing the process from terminating when you close your terminal window.) If a user’s network connection drops halfway through downloading the 19 GB qwen3-coder:30b model, what happens when they rerun the pull command? A. The download fails permanently, requiring them to delete the ollama directory and start from scratch. B. The ollama pull command is resumable, meaning the download picks up where it left off rather than starting over from 0%. C. Ollama automatically falls back to downloading the smaller llama3.1 model instead. D. The model gets corrupted, forcing the user to manually purge the cache using ollama clean before retrying. Correct Answer: B (Ollama’s pull command supports resumable downloads, saving users time and frustration if an interruption occurs during large model transfers.) In the command nohup ollama/bin/ollama serve, what is the role of the serve argument passed to the Ollama? A. It forces termination of active background sessions. B. It initializes and runs the local API server. C. It compiles the local source code into an executable. D. It downloads and installs the latest binary updates. Correct Answer: B (Passing the serve argument tells the Ollama executable to start up as an active API server ready to handle requests.)

Chapter 3 Explore data with gander Simplifying your data exploration with Local AI, gander and Tidyverse in RStudio 3.1 Learning Objectives Configure gander package with a local AI model and create a keyboard shortcut in RStudio Import genomics datasets from Google Cloud Storage into your AnVIL workspace and load onto RStudio Explore the count matrix and sample metadata with gander and tidyverse 3.2 Configure gander All commands in this section must be executed in the R Console (not inside Terminal). 3.2.1 Install and load required packages Run the following code in the R Console # AI integration packages install.packages("gander") library(gander) 3.2.2 Configure gander’s chat model To connect the gander package to your local Ollama server running the AI model, set the default option to your chat connection: options(gander.chat = chat) 3.2.3 Setup keyboard shortcut for gander Setting a keyboard shortcut allows you to invoke gander instantly inside your code editor without manually typing console commands. Create a gander shortcut: In RStudio: Navigate to Tools → Modify Keyboard Shortcuts Search for “gander” Assign a convenient shortcut: Shift+Cmd+g (macOS) 3.2.4 Test gander shortcut Your RStudio session now has an AI research partner that lives on your AnVIL instance. Let’s put it to work. Instead of jumping back and forth to an external browser chat window, gander reads your active code context and environment variables directly inside the IDE. How to use gander shortcut: In a clean R Script: Highlight - an object to query (or word, a sentence, code or an empty space). Evoke gander - using your pre-set shortcut Shift+Cmd+g. Enter a prompt - a short, concrete instruction of what you want to do in plain language. Review output Ask AI a question via gander shortcut. In a clean R Script: Highlight: options(gander.chat = chat) Evoke gander shortcut: Shift+Cmd+g Enter text prompt: “Briefly explain this code for me” Review the output - e.g. output code before running the generated code Sample gander output: This code sets a global option in R that tells the gander package which chat object to use for interactive AI assistance. The gander package is designed to help with data analysis by providing AI-powered insights and explanations. By setting options(gander.chat = chat), you're connecting gander to an existing chat session (likely initialized with a language model provider like OpenAI or Ollama) so that when you run gander commands, they can use this pre-established chat connection for communication with the language model. Interface Options: Choosing Replace means that the output will replace your highlighted text. Other options include Prefix (placed before your highlighted text) or Suffix (placed after your highlighted text.) 3.2.5 Quiz What is the primary benefit of using gander over a standard web-based AI chat window? A. It automatically uploads all of your local workspace files to a public cloud server for global sharing. B. It brings the AI assistant directly into your IDE workflow, allowing it to seamlessly evaluate your local R objects and script context without manual copy-pasting. C. It forces Ollama to bypass your CPU entirely and store 100% of large models within standard RAM. D. It permanently replaces the R Console with an automated script executor that runs code without user supervision. Correct Answer: B (gander is built specifically for data scientists to reduce friction by integrating AI into RStudio. Because it links with packages like ellmer and your local session, it can automatically detect your active R environment objects and surrounding code context.) Why would you want to keep your script lean and open a new .R script containing only the necessary code when asking Gander for help? A. To automatically install missing Bioconductor package dependencies. B. To prevent background code clutter from sending unrelated context and confusing the assistant. C. To permanently save your workspace environment variables to disk. D. To ensure your API key remains hidden from the R console history. Correct Answer: B (A long script sends a pile of unrelated code, adding unnecessary context noise). What happens if you forget to run the command “options(gander.chat = chat)” before trying to use gander in RStudio? A. The keyboard shortcut will open a web browser to a public AI chat window instead. B. gander won’t know where to send your prompts, similar to having a phone plugged in without dialing a number. C. R will throw a syntax error and automatically shut down the background Ollama server. D. The package will default to using a slower cloud-based model via the internet. Correct Answer: B (Running options(gander.chat = chat) connects the gander package directly to your local Ollama chat connection. Without it, gander has no designated target for your prompts, meaning it cannot route your questions to your local AI model. After leaving your RStudio session open on AnVIL, you step away and it automatically terminates after 30 minutes of inactivity. When you return the next day and resume working without having manually shut anything down, you run your script and encounter this error: “Error in chat_ollama(…) : could not find function”chat_ollama” A. The Ollama background server process stopped overnight, uninstalling all R packages from the container. B. The container restarted due to the inactivity timeout, meaning the R session started fresh and the ellmer package (containing chat_ollama) was no longer loaded. C. RStudio restored a saved workspace from yesterday, which preserved your environment variables but uninstalled all packages. D. The Sys.getenv() function timed out and corrupted the local R environment’s function namespace. Correct Answer: B (The container restarted due to the inactivity timeout, meaning the R session started fresh and the ellmer package containing chat_ollama was no longer loaded in memory.) 3.3 Import Data 3.3.1 Install and load required packages Run the following code in the R Console # AnVIL packages BiocManager::install("AnVILGCP") library(AnVILGCP) 3.3.2 Import data from Google Cloud Storage There are many ways to bring in data into RStudio on AnVIL. On ways to bring, import or access data on AnVIL see Data on AnVIL webbook. Here, we will bring in data from the existing Google bucket associated with an AnVIL workspace. Copy the airway dataset files (counts and metadata) from an AnVIL workspace bucket: gcloud_storage( "cp gs://fc-493d543d-3286-48ad-aeec-0bcb84b06fe5/airwaycounts.csv . " ) gcloud_storage( "cp gs://fc-493d543d-3286-48ad-aeec-0bcb84b06fe5/sample_metadata.csv . " ) In the RStudio ‘Files’ pane (bottom-right), confirm that airwaycounts.csv and sample_metadata.csv are now present in your working directory. 3.3.3 Load Data into R Load counts and metadata into R counts <- read.csv("airwaycounts.csv", row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE) metadata <- read.csv("sample_metadata.csv", row.names = 1 ) We load these files in this way to meet the formatting required by DESeq2 later on, ensuring the count matrix file is compatible with the metadata file: row.names = 1 (Counts): Sets the first column of the counts file (Ensembl IDs) as the row names. check.names = FALSE (Counts): Prevents R from altering sample names by default (e.g., converting characters like dashes into dots.) row.names = 1 (Metadata): Sets the first column of the metadata file (sample IDs) as the row names. Inspect your files manually in Console head(counts) head(metadata) 3.3.4 Quiz Which package moves files between the workspace bucket and the RStudio instance? A. DESeq2 B. gander C. AnVILGCP D. ellmer Correct Answer: C (AnVILGCP package, a core AnVIL package, provides specialized functions like gsutil_cp() to coordinate data transfers from Google bucket and the persistent disk of an RStudio environment) In the command gcloud_storage( "cp gs://fc-493d543d-3286-48ad-aeec-0bcb84b06fe5/airwaycounts.csv . " ), what is the correct prefix required to specify the Google Cloud Storage bucket path? A. cp B. gs:// C. fc- D. . Correct Answer: B (the prefix gs:// is required by Google Cloud utilities to recognize and access a cloud storage bucket. Following the gs://, the fc-493d543d-…string represents your unique workspace project ID/bucket name, while cp is the copy command itself, and ‘.’ represents the local destination directory.) 3.4 Inspect data with gander shortcut 3.4.1 Inspect counts file In a clean R Script, highlight the target variable or file name and provide a prompt. HIGHLIGHT: counts PROMPT: View counts sample gander output View(counts) Note, gander output may and likely will vary. For example, and alternative output to the same short ‘View counts’ prompt might be simply counts In a clean R Script, highlight the target variable or file name and provide a prompt. HIGHLIGHT: counts PROMPT: summarize counts stats sample gander output summarize(counts, across(everything(), list(mean = mean, sd = sd, min = min, max = max))) Use gander_peek() to check captured context In the R Console, type gander_peek() to see what gander saw: Based on the peek output, the assistant captures: Active file context: The object or file currently in focus (e.g., counts). User request: The explicit prompt provided (e.g., summarize counts stats). R environment snapshot: A preview of the object’s structure (e.g., data frame layout). Assistant decision: The generated output based on the observed context. Ask gander to explain code Leverage gander to break down unfamiliar logic, functions, or script sections directly within your workflow. HIGHLIGHT: summarize(counts, across(everything(), list(mean = mean, sd = sd, min = min, max = max))) PROMPT: Briefly explain this code sample gander output: This code calculates summary statistics (mean, standard deviation, minimum, and maximum) for all columns in the counts data frame. The across(everything()) selects all columns, and list() applies all four summary functions to each column simultaneously, returning a single row with all statistics arranged in columns. 3.4.2 Inspect metadata file with gander shortcut In a clean R Script, highlight the target variable or file name and provide a prompt. HIGHLIGHT: metadata PROMPT: View my metadata file sample gander output metadata In a clean R Script, highlight the target variable or file name and provide a prompt. HIGHLIGHT: metadata PROMPT: List all variables in my metadata sample gander output: SampleName, cell, dex, albut, Run, avgLength, Experiment, Sample, BioSample 3.4.3 Quiz When you highlight the object name ‘counts’ in your R script and invoke ‘gander’ with the prompt ‘View counts’, how does gander =generate a meaningful output? A. It queries a public online database of human genetic sequences via an external API. B. It resets your R session memory to clear any conflicting variables. C. It reads your active code context and inspects your local R workspace environment to understand what the counts object contains. D. It automatically installs and runs the DESeq2 package in the background. Correct Answer: C (gander leverages Integrated environment context integration, allowing it to inspect active script variables and query your local R environment directly without requiring you to manually copy and paste data into an external chat box.) 3.5 Explore data with gander and tydiverse 3.5.1 Install and Load Required Packages Run the following code in the R Console: # Common R tools for data manipulation and analysis install.packages("tidyverse") library(tidyverse) 3.5.2 Explore counts file with gander and tidyverse Inspect counts file. In a clean R Script: HIGHLIGHT: counts PROMPT: Explore my counts file with tydiverse sample gander output: counts %>% rownames_to_column(var = "gene") %>% pivot_longer(cols = -gene, names_to = "sample", values_to = "count") %>% group_by(sample) %>% summarize(total_counts = sum(count)) %>% arrange(desc(total_counts)) After running the above code, here is the output: # A tibble: 8 × 2 sample total_counts <chr> <int> 1 SRR1039517 30818215 2 SRR1039512 25348649 3 SRR1039516 24448408 4 SRR1039521 21164133 5 SRR1039508 20637971 6 SRR1039520 19126151 7 SRR1039509 18809481 8 SRR1039513 15163415 Ask specific questions. In a clean R Script: HIGHLIGHT: counts PROMPT: What is the library size of each sample? Use tidyverse sample gander output: counts %>% summarise_all(sum) %>% gather(sample, count) %>% mutate(count = as.numeric(count)) %>% group_by(sample) %>% summarise(lib_size = sum(count)) Ask another specific questions. In a clean R Script: HIGHLIGHT: counts PROMPT: How many genes (rows) have zero counts across every single sample in the dataset? Use tidyverse counts %>% rowSums() %>% {sum(. == 0)} Ask to explain code line by line. In a clean R Script: HIGHLIGHT: counts %>% rowSums() %>% {sum(. == 0)} PROMPT: Minimally annotate this code line by line sample gander output: # Sum rows to get total counts per gene # Count how many genes have zero expression across all samples # This gives the number of genes with no expression in any sample 3.5.3 Explore metadata file with gander and tidyverse Inspect metadata file with tidyverse. In a clean R Script: HIGHLIGHT: metadata PROMPT: Explore my metadata file with tydiverse sample gander output: metadata %>% group_by(cell, dex) %>% summarise( count = n(), avg_length = mean(avgLength), .groups = "drop" ) %>% arrange(desc(count)) After running this code, here is the output: # A tibble: 8 × 4 cell dex count avg_length <chr> <chr> <int> <dbl> 1 N052611 trt 1 87 2 N052611 untrt 1 126 3 N061011 trt 1 98 4 N061011 untrt 1 101 5 N080611 trt 1 126 6 N080611 untrt 1 120 7 N61311 trt 1 126 8 N61311 untrt 1 126 Ask a specific question. In a clean R Script: HIGHLIGHT: metadata PROMPT: How does avg_length compare between treated and untreated conditions? Use tidyverse sample gander output: metadata %>% group_by(dex) %>% summarize(avg_length = mean(avgLength)) After running this code, here is the output: # A tibble: 2 × 2 dex avg_length <chr> <dbl> 1 trt 109. 2 untrt 118. 3.5.4 Quiz What is the sequence and best practice when interacting with the AI assistant gander in RStudio? A. Open a blank script, type your prompt in plain language, and automatically execute the generated code. B. Open a blank script, highlight a specific object of query, invoke gander with the shortcut, enter a short and concrete prompt, and carefully review the output before running the generated code. C. Trigger the shortcut first, type a broad multi-task instruction like “do all my RNA-seq analysis,” and let the AI overwrite your workspace files. D. Skip highlighting any objects, use the shortcut to launch a local Ollama server, and let the model automatically push results to GitHub. Correct Answer: B (Using gander effectively follows starting with a clean script, highlighting the specific object of interest to provide environment context, invoking the shortcut, supplying a concrete instruction, and reviewing the returned code before execution.) When working with tidyverse pipelines in R, what is the primary role of the pipe operator (%>%)? A. It permanently saves intermediate data frames to the hard drive as CSV files. B. It forwards the output of one function directly into the first argument of the next function. C. It connects your local R session to the remote Google Cloud Storage bucket. D. It automatically installs missing packages like DESeq2 from Bioconductor. Correct Answer: B (The pipe operator (%>%) chains data operations together by passing the expression on its left-hand side as the primary argument to the function on its right-hand side.) When you highlight a snippet of tidyverse code and ask gander to “Minimally annotate this code line by line”, what AI capability is primarily being demonstrated? A. Natural language code comprehension, allowing the local AI to interpret complex syntax and translate its logic into human-readable comments. B. Automated neural network model retraining using your live sequencing data. C. Automatic compilation of R code into high-speed machine learning algorithms. D. Instantaneous translation of R scripts into Python Pandas syntax. Correct Answer: A (gander uses the local large language model to parse code syntax and semantics, enabling it to explain, document, or annotate code snippets contextually right inside your environment.)
